lions.headline: Detroit Lions offer firm defense of Brian Branch’s play despite fines
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 01: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) takes the field prior to the Detroit Lions versus Minnesota Vikings game on Sunday November 1, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

In his first game back, Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch received a fine for improper use of his helmet on this play against Packers tight end Tucker Kraft.

Hey @nfl can y'all do something about this??? pic.twitter.com/2CKGCkTsbS
— Easton Butler (@Easton__Butler) October 25, 2026

The following week, Branch had another helmet-to-helmet collision, this time with teammate DJ Wonnum. The collision knocked both Wonnum and Branch out of the game with a concussion.

#BrianBranch #DJWonnum
Both @Lions players to locker room
One carted, one on own power
2 head injury checks from friendly fire pic.twitter.com/yCsiIoB20r
— David J. Chao – ProFootballDoc (@ProFootballDoc) November 1, 2026

Violent collisions with his helmet are nothing new with Branch. He’s been fined six times for impermissible use of his helmet, twice for hit on a defenseless receiver, and he was ejected from a game after a particularly violent head-to-head collision vs. the Packers in 2024.

Despite the two notable collisions through two games, Lions safeties coach Jim O’Neil offered an impassioned defense of Branch’s play.

“We coach eyes-up tackle, but we also coach—we’re going to play the game violently,” O’Neil said. “That’s the way the game was meant to play. That’s one of the reasons BB is who he is. I mean, he’s got an old-school mentality. He’s explosive. He’s going to play the game violently. We talk about defending every blade of grass, whether it’s on the sideline—you’re not going to tiptoe the sideline on us. If a running back’s on his way down, we’re going to beat him to the ground and hit him.

“I thought BB did a great job on that play. He lowered his target. Obviously, when the receiver drops, as well, sometimes it’s head-to-head. We’ll continue to coach eyes-up tackle, but I love the way Brian Branch plays, and we’re not going to do anything to change that. We’re going to continue to try to help him with his technique, but we’re not going to change his mentality at all.”

Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell made a similar argument about Branch.

“Once he’s going, he’s going for his target and then that target drops. And so, that ends up where it goes,” Campbell said. “You can certainly say go lower, but now you have got to be careful. You start going real low, then you start taking out knees and stuff, and you don’t want any of that. So, just keep your eyes up, see what you hit, try to drop it just a little bit.”

Branch is progressing through concussion protocol, and barring any setback, the Lions expect him to play this week vs. the Miami Dolphins. That’s good news for Detroit, because O’Neil compared Branch’s versatility to having three extra players on defense.

“I think as we get into the third, fourth, fifth game here, he’s going to catch his groove,” O’Neil said. “He’s such a unique piece, because he can play like a linebacker, he can play like a corner, he can play like a safety. It’s like having three extra guys up on game day, because of what he can do for the defense.”

lions.headline: Lions vs. Dolphins: 3 key matchups
lions.body:
The Detroit Lions (5-2) take their talents to South Beach to take on the Miami Dolphins (1-6). Fresh off a three-game win streak, including two in a row against the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, the Lions have reestablished themselves as true NFC North contenders.

Despite the back-to-back-to-back victories, the Lions still find themselves currently in third place in the division. This week, the Chicago Bears take on the rising Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Minnesota Vikings host Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on “Monday Night Football.” If the Lions take care of their business, there is a realistic opportunity that Dan Campbell’s team will sit alone at the top of the standings.

From just about every performance and talent metric, the Lions should have the edge in this matchup. But digging deeper, the Dolphins are rebuilding in a way that should remind Lions fans of the Dan Campbell led 2021 team.

In what could typically be labeled a “trap game,” often the NFL rears its powerful element of parity into the equation. To avoid that, the key matchups will come down to not necessarily the talent on the field, the grit of the players to determine the ultimate outcome.

Let’s dive in to the three key matchups centered on the intangible traits that will make or break Sunday’s matchup in south Florida.

Gritty rookies in key roles

Breaking the normal structure of the article here as this first key matchup really is not a direct positional or players matchup, but the comparative play of the key rookies on each team. While many readers here at Pride of Detroit are familiar the Grit Index, for newer readers, it is the NFL Draft metric that Erik Schlitt and I have created to grade prospects on their intangible qualities.

In the 2026 NFL Draft, seven teams drafted players in the elite tier of the Grit Index with a score of 9+. The Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins were two of those teams.

There were 30 players with a 9+ score on this year’s GRIT Index (top ~7.5%)

Only 2 teams drafted 3 or more players within this Elite tier:

— Chicago (4 – Thieneman, Roush, Jones, Elliott)
— Detroit (3 – Miller, Abney, Gill-Howard)

(2 – BAL, IND, LV, MIA, PIT)
— Between The Numbers – Anthony (@BtwnTheNumbers) April 26, 2026

For the Lions, it was Blake Miller, Keith Abney, and Skyler Gill-Howard. For the Dolphins, it was Jacob Rodriguez and Michael Taaffe.

You could call it coincidence, but I am not surprised that each of these five rookies have become key contributors for their respective teams. In fact, Rodriguez and Taaffe are first and second, respectively, in snaps played on the entire Dolphins roster. Similarly, Miller, Abney, and Gill-Howard lead the Lions 2026 rookie draft class in snap counts on the season.

They key here with all five of these players is which one will either rise to the occasion, or which one will be a potential liability? Rookies go through growing pains and not all progress is linear. Will Taaffe rise to the occasion against the Lions elite offensive weapons? Will Rodriguez command and communicate the defense to his teammates as the green dot linebacker against the creatively-detailed Lions offense run by offensive coordinator Drew Petzing and Jared Goff?

Will the Lions rookies take their strong starts to the next level, or will it be a game filled with growing pains coming off a three-game win streak?

The play of these rookies will go a long way in determining the outcome of the game.

The Lions’ linebacker room

This is a big week. At this point, we’re all aware of and have been in the emotional waiting room following the updates and progression after Jack Campbell’s traumatic neck injury against the Vikings. The impact, though, is most significantly felt by those players closest to him.

The key matchup is not how fellow linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske fill in Jack Campbell’s shoes, no player will be able to do that for this team. And I don’t suspect they are trying to.

The key is how Barnes, Rodriguez, and Nowaske can play as the best version of themselves and as a unit while battling this adversity on and off the field.

Derrick Barnes wept in the locker room. Malcolm Rodriguez spent the first night "hugging my family." Even Alex Anzalone was hurting in Tampa Bay.

But the season continues, and "he doesn’t want us to feel sorry for him."

"Prepare and play like 46." https://t.co/Fv9KTOtsMo
— Will Burchfield (@burchie_kid) November 5, 2026

In my view, having Kelvin Sheppard as defensive coordinator, former linebacker coach, and former linebacker himself, he is in a unique position to lead these players through this storm. Sheppard has expressed nothing but confidence in the group.

“I raised these other guys that are about to play. Malcolm Rodriguez and Derrick Barnes, those are my little brothers and they know the standard. They both have worn the green dot before. So, this isn’t like a first-time ordeal for either one of them, because that load might get shared. We’re still working through that, but I’m confident in either one of them.”

I don’t expect this group to be perfect as each player adapts to their adjusted roles. But I do expect each to play with passion and grit. I expect them to prepare and play like 46.

Zach Sieler vs. Lions interior offensive line

Lastly, turning to the leader of the Dolphins, captain Zach Sieler is not only the fins most disruptive player on defense, he is the heart and soul of the team.

🎥 Jeff Hafley on Zach Sieler's leadership: "It's valuable to me, it's valuable to the young players… he's one of the best people ever. There's not a much better person out there than Zach Sieler. He does everything the right way." (@MiamiDolphins) #PhinsUp pic.twitter.com/gal8hkUSCF
— FinsXtra (@FinsXtra) October 5, 2026

Dan Campbell has emphasized Sieler’s impact.

“Defensively, Sieler’s really the anchor in there. You know, he’s played good football for a really long time, man. Smart, crafty, powerful, can get an edge in the pass game.”

Relentless in both the run and pass game, Sieler will present a challenge to the youth of the Lions interior offensive line. With starting center Cade Mays not practicing and a wave of injuries on defense, the Lions can control the game if Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, and Tate Ratledge can continue to win the line of scrimmage along the interior.

In a game where, On Paper, the Lions have a distinct advantage, players like Sieler can lead the charge in a spoiler’s effort.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities for grit to win the day.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Dolphins 5 Qs preview: Is Miami mirroring Detroit’s 2021 culture rebuild?
lions.body:
Dan Campbell guides the Lions through workouts during a spring minicamp. 2022-06-10 Dan Campbell | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions head to South Beach for a Week 9 interconference matchup against a young, rebuilding Miami Dolphins team.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Kevin Nogle, the Managing Editor of Phinsider to give us some insight into this Miami team ahead of Sunday’s kickoff. We learned about the local sentiment surrounding head coach Jeff Hafley’s foundational reset, how offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik is tailoring the offense to quarterback Malik Willis, and how Ollie Gordon is handling the backfield workload in De’Von Achane’s absence—plus what Miami needs to do to keep pace with Detroit’s offense.

1. Miami arguably made more changes to their organization than any other team in the NFL this offseason. New head coach, new quarterback, the changing out of long-tenured skill position players—it was a massive overhaul in South Beach.

Although the Dolphins are off to a 1-6 start, how much of that was expected from a team that underwent so many changes this offseason? It’s early, but do you get the sense that new head coach Jeff Hafley is the right guy for this rebuild?

This year is about setting up the franchise for the future, and while losses are never fun, the struggles were expected. This is the league’s youngest team, and they are facing a steep learning curve. Miami has 14 rookies on the roster, plus another seven first-year players. This is clearly a reset of the team’s foundation, and there will be growing pains.

The Dolphins’ schedule has also been brutal this year. They started the year against the Las Vegas Raiders, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs, and Minnesota Vikings, not facing a team that had a loss until Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals, who were 2-2 coming into that game. Through Week 8, Miami has faced the league’s toughest schedule, with a combined opponent winning percentage of .589. The schedule is not an excuse, but with such a young team, it is another variable to consider.

Obviously, things can change, but Hafley has instilled confidence in the fanbase so far. The Mike McDaniel era had some fun moments, but it quickly fell apart and the team never adjusted (and McDaniel still does not seem to have made adjustments as the Los Angeles Chargers struggle this year). I think Hafley’s focus on making the Dolphins physical, allowing the younger players to gain experience, and the team’s ability to make adjustments, learn from mistakes, and continue to fight even in losing situations indicate he is the right guy for this role. Lions fans saw Dan Campbell build a culture out of tough losses back in 2021; that is exactly the phase Hafley and the Dolphins are in right now.

2. From the outside looking in, Malik Willis was dropped into a tough situation given the pieces around him in the offense—and it looks like, predictably, the passing game has struggled so far. The Dolphins rank 26th in passing DVOA and EPA/pass.

How has Bobby Slowik tried to tailor this offense to Willis’ strengths? What’s working, what’s not working, and how much of that is related to a new quarterback in a new system versus the lack of talent personnel-wise?

I think we are starting to see Willis find some comfort in the offensive system, and he is starting to play better. Despite being a third-round pick in 2022, Willis has played in only 29 career games, starting just 13. He is a league veteran but really has the starting experience of a rookie. At times, he still seems bothered by the speed of the game, but the experience he is getting this year is already making a difference in his play.

I think one of the biggest issues we have seen from Willis is a desire to be a pocket passer. He stays in the pocket longer than he should, trying to find the perfect pass rather than taking something shorter or throwing the ball away to avoid a sack. The offensive line is not doing him any favors, but he has taken multiple sacks by running out of bounds instead of throwing the ball away. He seemed to want to avoid using his legs, but has opened up that part of his game in the last couple of weeks.

Slowik, like McDaniel before him, has an offensive system built on quarterback accuracy and timing. He uses bootlegs, run-pass options, and play-action passes to get Willis out of the pocket and seeing open receivers. They also seem to be using some half-field concepts, keeping Willis looking in one area and working from deep to shallow rather than having him search the entire field for receivers.

The youth on the roster – especially with wide receivers Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman Jr. – do not always create separation, and drops have also been an issue. When the primary target is not open on time, a young quarterback hesitates, and behind an evolving offensive line, hesitation leads to sacks. That all relates back to the discussion of Miami’s reset this year. The potential for talent is on Miami’s roster, but they still need to grow individually and together. The coaching staff is clearly working on the balance between youth and system – relying on a more basic system as the players learn.

3. Losing De’Von Achane in the first month of the season felt especially cruel for this offense that was already so limited on difference makers. The Dolphins rank 9th in EPA/rush (-0.03) but rank near the bottom of the league in rush success rate (26th) and rush DVOA (26th), suggesting that their run game is a boom-or-bust attack.

Is that a fair assessment of Ollie Gordon’s performance this year? The Dolphins also rank 26th in stuffed rate (22.8%) which is the percentage of runs that earn zero or negative yards. Are those stuffed runs more of an indictment of the offensive line or the coaching/play calling?

That seems like a fair assessment. Gordon has been a lot of fun to watch as he breaks out this year, but he is a power-back who works extremely well as a change-of-pace option behind Achane. When he finds space, he is able to break it for a big gain, but it really is boom or bust on each run.

Part of that is Gordon and his abilities. Part of that is the offensive line finding space to get him free. And part of that is opposing defenses planning to stop the run. Miami has had success this year, averaging 131 rushing yards per game, and they have topped 100 yards in five of seven games, including one game over 150 yards and another over 200 yards. They also have two games with 74 yards rushing each. Boom or bust.

The offensive line—especially last week with Kadyn Proctor out with a concussion—still has work to do to come together as a unit.

I think play calling is part of it, but not necessarily because the plays are wrong, but rather because the player is wrong. The rushing attack was built for Achane’s skill set, complemented by Gordon. Now, it is a Gordon-led unit and some of the designs are clearly meant for Achane’s speed over Gordon’s power. We have seen that evolve as Slowik has adjusted to Gordon, but there is an obvious difference between the two players and there will likely be a boom or bust aspect to the Dolphins’ ground game all season. The outside zone, stretch concepts were designed for Achane’s elite sideline-to-sideline track speed. Gordon is a one-cut, downhill runner. The Dolphins have pivoted to more gap and inside-zone looks to match Gordon’s style, but until defenses are forced to back out of the box, stops will linger.

4. Hafley brings his decades of experience coaching defense to Miami, and the numbers related to personnel deployment and coverage usage are pretty interesting through eight weeks. Miami lines up in base personnel 51.7% of snaps, second-most in the NFL, and they’re utilizing zone coverage 78.8% of the time (10th in the NFL).

How much of these numbers overlap with the talent available on the current roster? In other words, does it feel like Hafley’s trying to put his players in the best spots to succeed? Numbers suggest the run defense is bordering on being a top-10 unit, but the pass defense might be the worst in the league. Do those numbers tell the whole story?

Hafley definitely relies on base defense and he expects his front four to create pressure, rather than relying on the blitz—especially when compared to someone like Brian Flores, a former Dolphins head coach, and his blitz heavy defense. Hafley expects the pressure to come from the front four, allowing him to keep additional players back in coverage or focused on the run. It has been successful—at least as successful as can be expected with the younger players executing on the field.

The run defense has been strong for much of the year. There have been mistakes, especially when an edge rusher bites on a play action, chasing the quarterback and failing to set the edge or runs right past the ball carrier, but overall, they are doing well against the run. Of course, I say all of that knowing full well Jahmyr Gibbs is second in the league in rushing and is averaging nearly five-yards-per-carry, so the pressure is on the defense to continue to find success this week.

Does the contrast between the pass defense and the run defense tell the entire story? Not necessarily. The heavy zone scheme with the younger defensive backs is designed to prevent explosive, 60+ yard plays. That is allowing for short and intermediate routes to pick apart defenses (especially when Miami struggles to cover tight ends. Good thing the Lions are not bringing a top-tier tight end into this game, right?!?). Add in that Miami has been playing from behind for much of the year, and the short, possession passing game has been highly effective.

I do think Hafley is keeping his defensive calls a little more basic than maybe we will see from him in the next few years, allowing the foundation to be set before he starts building off of it. The Dolphins have stressed that they expect to build for the future through the draft and grow the team from within. If they stick to that plan, I think you will see both the offense and defense evolve as the players grow and Miami moves from a roster dominated by rookies to one with veterans hitting their prime supported by key rookies each year.

5. The Dolphins opened as 7-point home underdogs over at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this Week 9 matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Dolphins on Sunday afternoon?

I want to see the offense be aggressive and take shots downfield. The Lions are allowing 276 yards per game through the air, and they are banged up. Let Willis test them early, get Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell into the game, and use the play-action to create opportunities. The Dolphins need to come into this game feeling like they have to win in a shoot-out. If they are aggressive on offense, maybe they can catch the Lions a little flat-footed at the start.

I need to see the Dolphins continue to make adjustments week-to-week, correct mistakes from the last game, and grow as a unit. That will be true throughout this season. Continued growth week to week is important and seeing the team not make the same mistakes over and over will continue to keep Dolphins fans confident the team is headed in the right direction.

I am sure I will see the Dolphins compete in this game and play hard through the fourth quarter. They may not be biting kneecaps (I love Dan Campbell and miss him in Miami), but they should be physical and give it everything they have on every down. I am also sure I will see Campbell continue to be aggressive on third- and fourth-down. The Dolphins have allowed over 50 percent conversion for opposing offenses on third down this year. They have to expect the Lions to attack on third down, and then attack again on fourth down.

The Lions are coming into this game as the better team. They should leave Miami having proven they are the better team. But, if Miami executes well, they can at least stand toe-to-toe with Detroit throughout the game, take the punches, and fight through the final bell. Really, the Dolphins have the ability to be the 2021 Lions – growing with a first-year head coach, taking a bad season and turning it into the foundation for a brighter future. If Miami can follow the same pathway as the Lions, this would be a successful rebuild.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview, prediction: On Paper
lions.body:
MIAMI, FL - OCTOBER 21: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Detroit Lions in action against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on October 21, 2018 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Mark Brown/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can’t afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear.

But is there a real chance of an upset in Miami, or are the Lions clearly the better team? Let’s examine it in our Lions vs. Dolphins preview and prediction. It’s time for On Paper.

Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Dolphins pass defense (29th)

The Lions’ passing offense remains one of their most reliable units on the team. While last week’s performance against the Vikings wasn’t explosive, it was certainly a lot better than most teams manage against Minnesota’s defense. While the DVOA ranking remains outside the top five, I still believe Detroit’s passing attack should be in that top tier.

For the season, they rank:

Fourth in passer rating (110.0)

Seventh in yards per attempt (7.9)

Third in dropback EPA (0.264)

First in EPA/pass (+0.21)

Fourth in dropback success rate (51.4%)

Detroit is humming in all facets of their passing attack. In pass protection, the Lions allow the fifth-lowest pressure percentage (30.1%), rank seventh in pass-block win rate (54%), and rank third in PFF team pass-blocking grade (75.1).

The Dolphins may have a worse pass defense than the Lions. Five out of the seven quarterbacks who have faced Miami have finished with a passer rating of 119.8 or higher. Granted, they’ve played some really good quarterbacks in Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Drake Maye. Still, those quarterbacks have outperformed their year-long efficiency against Miami, and the DVOA ranking—which adjusts to opponents’ strength—proves this is a bad pass defense.

Overall, they rank:

32nd in passer rating allowed (119.5)

32nd in yards per attempt (8.3)

32nd in dropback EPA (0.288)

32nd in dropback success rate (53.7%)

This is the result of having an extremely young and inexperienced back seven.

Though there is some recent hope for Miami’s pass rush. As Erik Schlitt pointed out in his Honolulu Blueprint, while the season-long stats don’t look great for the Dolphins’ ability to get to the passer (35.6% pressure rate, 18th; 4.2% sack rate, 28th), they’ve started to put things together. All nine of their sacks have come in the last four games, and they’ve posted a pressure rate of 39.5% or higher in three out of four of those games (league average is around 36%).

Over those last four games, the Dolphins’ pass defense has been better, but certainly not good. From Weeks 4-8, Miami ranks 27th in dropback EPA (0.180) and 29th in success rate (50.7%).

Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. It’s been a quiet few weeks for the Lions tight end, but Miami is allowing the sixth-highest yardage to tight ends (483 yards) and tied for the fourth-most touchdowns (six).

Advantage: Lions +3. This is a top-five unit vs. a bottom-five unit. The only reason I’m not giving it a higher advantage is that some things are trending Miami’s way, and weather could also play a factor, with some slight chance of rain.

Lions run offense (4th) vs. Dolphins run defense (26th)

The Lions’ rushing attack still has frustrating bouts of inconsistency, but last week’s performance against the Vikings felt like a revelation. Whether Detroit’s sidecar formation was a Vikings-specific answer or the cracking of the code for the entire season, we’ll see. But it shows one thing for certain: Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is capable of finding some answers.

For the season, the Lions rushing attack now ranks:

Ninth in yards per carry (4.6)

13th in rush EPA (-0.083)

Third in success rate (47.0%)

But I must continue to repeat myself that the negative plays are a big problem. The Lions’ 19.3% stuffed rate is sixth in the NFL. Those figures are down from last week (20.9%, third-highest), but it still remains an issue to track. Detroit’s power success rank also improved after last week, but they still rank just 24th, converting on just 59% of short-yardage situations.

Still, it’s worth pointing out how both the offensive line and the running backs are doing their parts. Detroit’s line ranks third in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and fourth in PFF run blocking grade. Meanwhile, Detroit’s backfield ranks sixth in rushing yards over expected per rush (+0.5), sixth in yards after contact per rush (3.38), and Jahmyr Gibbs ranks fourth in missed tackle forced rate (31.9%).

This chart doesn’t exactly vibe with the Dolphins’ bottom-10 DVOA ranking. They’re not giving up a ton of yards nor a ton of yards per carry. So what gives? Let’s look deeper.

Eighth in yards per carry allowed (3.8)

22nd in rush EPA (-0.078)

30th in rush success rate (43.9%)

In short, it appears the Dolphins don’t give up a ton of big, explosive plays, but they essentially give up exactly what the offense needs. That’s backed by data. Miami has only given up 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th), and just three rushes of 20+ yards (t-sixth fewest).

The good news is the Dolphins are weak where the Lions’ run offense struggles. They’ve produced just a 14.9% stuffed rate (23rd), and they rank 21st in power success rate, allowing conversions on 68% of short-yardage situations.

Player to watch: Jacob Rodriguez. The Dolphins rookie linebacker has been a fun player to watch thus far. Rodriguez has been credited with 30 “stops” per PFF (plays that are a failure for offense), which is second most among ALL NFL linebackers, not just rookies. Seventeen of those have come in the run, t-eighth most.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. I’m not sure I’d expect a huge game from Gibbs and company, given that Miami has not allowed over 150 rushing yards in a game. But Detroit should be fairly efficient on the ground.

Dolphins pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th)

It hasn’t been a great start to the year for Malik Willis in his new home, but it’s hard to blame him given the supporting cast. He’s got an extremely young receiving corps, a new offensive system, and an imbalanced offensive line. As a result, the Dolphins rank:

26th in passer rating (79.7)

20th in yards per attempt (6.9)

23rd in dropback EPA (0.014)

20th in dropback success rate (43.8%)

The Dolphins aren’t a complete disaster, but they’re clearly below average.

That said, there are some very interesting advanced statistics surrounding Willis. For one, he’s not afraid to chuck it deep. He currently owns the third-highest average depth of target (9.2), and his deep ball percentage of 16.4% ranks first in the NFL (yes, above Jordan Love, too). But he also ranks third in time to throw (3.05), suggesting he likely holds onto the ball too long—especially when you consider the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate (10.3%).

The offensive line is a mixed bag. Though they’ve allowed the second-highest pressure rate (43.2%), they rank 20th in pass block win rate and 31st in PFF pass blocking grade. The issue is that the left side of their offensive line is good-to-great (LT Patrick Paul is 14th in pass blocking grade, rookie LG Kadyn Proctor is improving) and the right side is a disaster (RT Austin Jackson is dead last in pass blocking grade, RG Jonah Savaiinaea is 63rd out of 76).

And as mentioned before, the receiving corps is ridiculously young: Malik Washington is 25; Caleb Douglas is 23, and Chris Bell is 22. Young doesn’t mean bad, but it’ll take them some time to get adjusted to the NFL.

Is the Lions’ pass defense actually getting better? It’s hard for me to tell. The raw numbers are improving, but as the chart above shows, they’ve also played some pretty bad passing offenses in the last few weeks. I’m not yet convinced.

Overall, the Lions rank:

26th in passer rating allowed (101.0)

18th in yards per attempt (7.3)

29th in dropback EPA (0.218)

28th in success rate (50.0%)

I think it’s also worth noting that the Lions’ pass rush has fallen off a bit as of late. After three weeks, the Lions ranked 10th in pressure rate (39.0%) and second in time to pressure (2.46). The Lions now rank just 17th in pressure rate (35.8%) and 20th in time to pressure (2.68). And this week, they’re almost certainly without DJ Wonnum, who was fourth on the team in pressures (14). That said, the Lions still do rank third in pass rush win rate, third in PFF pass rush grade, and seventh in sack rate. I just worry it’s trending in the wrong direction.

Then, of course, there are the injuries to account for. While it looks like Brian Branch is on track to play, the Lions don’t have MIKE linebacker Jack Campbell, and top cornerback D.J. Reed is trending toward missing this game. Detroit’s back seven has already struggled immensely in coverage, and now they’ll be tested further.

Player to watch: Malik Washington. Washington leads the Dolphins in catches (31) and yards (329), and the Dolphins like to use him all over the field—as a screen weapon or downfield. His 4.47 speed is a weapon.

Advantage: Draw. I’m not particularly impressed with either unit. I think it’s certainly possible Willis hits on a few big downfield plays, and I think it’s also very possible Detroit is able to disrupt and sack Willis 4-6 times this game. In the end, I think it’ll all even out.

Dolphins run offense (26th) vs. Lions run defense (23rd)

This is another weird statistical oddity for Miami. By the charts, it looks like they actually have a good thing going with their run game, including a breakout season from Ollie Gordon (408 yards, 4.5 YPC, 4 TDs) and some quarterback rushing potential from Malik Willis (225 yards, 3 TDs). Yet, the advanced statistics aren’t as impressive. They rank:

11th in yards per carry (4.4)

21st in rush EPA (-0.128)

24th in success rate (36.0%)

It turns out this rushing attack is very boom or bust—like a less-efficient version of Detroit’s running game. They have produced t-sixth-most rushes of 10+ yards (26), but also a 19.1% stuff rate—seventh-highest.

The problem appears to be that the offensive line isn’t carrying their end of the bargain. They rank 26th in run block win rate, 27th in PFF run blocking grade, and 27th in adjusted line yards.

But credit to Gordon for doing everything he can to get the most out of his situation.

I don’t know, man. The Lions are just too inconsistent in the run game this year. They’ve been better lately, but it seems like they’re still susceptible to explosive plays. Overall, the Lions rank:

16th in yards per carry allowed (4.1)

17th in rush EPA (-0.096)

11th in success rate (37.2%)

So that pretty much matches my eye test. They’re decent down-to-down, but they give up too many explosives. Though they’ve only allowed 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th fewest), they’ve allowed six of 20+ yards (t-ninth most).

And with the loss of Jack Campbell, it’s hard to know how this unit will respond. Detroit has an experienced linebacking corps in Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske, but none provide the instincts and consistency of Campbell.

Player to watch: Tyleik Williams. I pointed it out in my Dolphins vs. Patriots thoughts, but Miami really struggled against New England’s nose tackle last week, and Williams remains an impossible guy to move.

Advantage: Dolphins +1. I’m giving Miami a slight advantage here for a couple of reasons. First, I am concerned about the loss of Jack Campbell, and it may take a couple of weeks for Detroit to find a plan that works without him. Second, I do think Willis provides a legitimate rushing threat, and Detroit has lost contain far too often this year. Third, I just think Miami is better than their stats suggest, and the Lions may be a tad worse. It shouldn’t be a dominant day for Miami—and if Detroit can get out to a big lead, they can erase this advantage completely—but I still think Miami has the slight edge here.

Last week’s prediction:

On Paper drops to 5-2 overall and 3-4 against the spread, but I don’t feel all that bad for how my Lions vs. Vikings preview played out. The only area I made a clear mistake was underestimating the Lions’ run game, and for the first half of that game, I looked right. But Petzing made a lot of believers on Sunday, and I’m one of them.

In the comment section, we nearly had two perfect predictions, despite the odd score. Muddy.D’s 19-16 Lions prediction was just a single point away, as was Devil Barrel’s 18-15 Lions prediction. Here is your prize. Share it, or I’ll take it back, and you get nothing.

It’s a football lasso. Just in case you happen to commit the awful sin of spinning a football near an opponent, you can rope it back in before any ref sees!

This week’s prediction:

The Lions come out with a pretty definitive +3.5 advantage. I know the Dolphins have kept it close with some recent opponents, but I’m not really buying it. There isn’t a single thing they do particularly well, and their worst unit (pass defense) happens to match up with Detroit’s best unit (pass offense). I think that could spell disaster for Miami, as they don’t want Malik Willis dropping back 50 times to try and keep pace with Jared Goff.

I think we get our first comfortable Lions win since the Cardinals game. Lions 38, Dolphins 24.

michigan.headline: 3 Keys to Victory: Michigan Football vs. Michigan State
michigan.body:
The Battle for Paul Bunyan is here, as Michigan Football will host a Michigan State team that has lost six straight, is winless in Big Ten play and is on a four-year losing streak to the Wolverines. Despite history not being on their side, the Spartans are sure to bring the physicality and intensity known in the in-state rivalry.

Here the keys to victory for Michigan to walk away with the Paul Bunyan Trophy for the fifth straight year.

Make field goals

This one is pretty self explanatory. Head coach Kyle Whittingham said there would be a kicking competition this week after sophomore Trey Butkowski missed two field goals against Rutgers and two field goals against Indiana. Although the Wolverines came out on top against the Scarlet Knights, the same can’t be said for the game against the Hoosiers — and those two kicks likely cost Michigan the game.

Butkowski was only called on for a field goal four times in the first six weeks before attempting that many in just one game against Indiana. But when playing in a game that relies on the productivity of your defense and taking advantage of short fields, even if just a field goal, the kicking unit has to be able to convert.

In what will likely be a low scoring game between Michigan and Michigan State, converting on field goals could be the difference between a win and a loss. No matter who’s taking the attempts, they simply need to go through the uprights.

Finally get the run game going

A key stat that is getting thrown around when talking about the in-state rivalry is the team with more rushing yards has won 49 of the last 56 matchups.

Both teams have struggled this season running the ball. Michigan State is 113th in the country with 110.1 rushing yards, while Michigan is 84th with 138 rushing yards per game. A major problem for the Wolverines has been simply playing a game with their offensive line healthy. Thus far, the offensive line has had to constantly rotate lineups due to injury and really hasn’t been able to establish a rhythm.

Michigan found moderate success when handing the ball off to Savion Hiter 20 times for 79 yards against Rutgers, but the Wolverines will need to improve on their 3.6 yards per carry from a game ago. Freshman quarterback Tommy Carr has created opportunities for himself with his legs, but to establish the run game would allow even more possibilities for more play action and quarterback designed runs to become even more effective, not to mention having more manageable down and distances.

Pressure the quarterback, whoever it is

Michigan State is decimated by injuries, particularly on offense. The Spartans will be without their top two running backs on an offense that already puts up just 291.4 yards per game (129th in the FBS). They also rank 113th in both rushing yards and passing yards.

Michigan football availability report vs. Michigan State: pic.twitter.com/H1F53RI6ce
— Alejandro Zúñiga (@ByAZuniga) November 5, 2026

Starting quarterback Alessio Milivojevic is also questionable for the game, but no matter if it’s him or freshman Kayd Coffman, the focus for Michigan’s defense should be to make that quarterback uncomfortable. The Spartans allow three sacks per game, which ranks 105th overall.

As mentioned in the previous key, the run game has been instrumental to winning the Paul Bunyan Trophy. So if the Michigan defense can shut down the pass game and have the Spartans start to rely on their run game — which is already looking for production from someone deep on the depth chart — it could make for a long night for Michigan State’s offense.

michigan.headline: What they’re saying Week 10: MSU in ‘deepest hole ever’ according to one national writer
michigan.body:
EAST LANSING, MI - OCTOBER 17: Michigan State Spartans head coach Pat Fitzgerald looks toward the scoreboard during a college football game between the Michigan State Spartans and Northwestern Wildcats on October 17, 2026 at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing, MI. (Photo by Adam Ruff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

It’s a big one on Saturday night as the state title is on the line when the Michigan Wolverines host the Michigan State Spartans in the Big House. The maize and blue have captured four straight in this rivalry and are currently near two touchdown favorites over an injured Spartan squad that will likely be down to their third quarterback in this matchup. Heading into tonight’s contest, streamed on Peacock for the national audience, here’s what the players, coaches, fans, and media are saying about The Battle for the Paul Bunyan Trophy.

National view: Michigan State in “deepest hole ever”

The Athletic released a long-form piece about the state of Michigan State football, calling it their “deepest hole ever” following the Mel Tucker and Larry Nassar scandals, countless leadership turnover in the athletic department, and the complete lack of success on the football field.

New Athletic Director: “Where we are in football is not OK, and it’s not (Pat Fitzgerald’s) fault,” Dan Bartholomae told The Athletic. “We’re going to build a support system around him and get this done.”

Like Kyle Whittingham in Ann Arbor, Fitzgerald is in his first year with the Spartans off to a 2-6 start, no conference wins, and a flurry of detrimental injuries to his roster. That’s gotten in the way of a roster that the Spartans have reportedly invested over $20 million dollars into according to The Athletic. It’s something that the new head coach thinks he can build upon. “From my perspective, there’s a feeling around here that we understand what it’s gonna take to win and how we need to go about that process,” said Fitzgerald. “When we get that second class together, really my first full recruiting class, now you’re putting multiple layers of guys in the locker room who only know one way to do it.”

From the Michigan perspective, the team coming into Ann Arbor on Saturday is one that is desperate for a signature win to build upon. Many have said this is the Spartans’ Super Bowl. This year might be even more than that: a propeller forward. Michigan’s nearly two-touchdown favorites. They cannot afford to give this Spartan program life. The winner gets bragging rights for 365 days, and the current state of the Wolverines’ program could really use something like that over their in-state rivals when there is already so little going for them.

From the locker room: Michigan leaders ready for a physical fight

“It’s going to be a physical-ass game,” Jon Jansen said to Michigan TE Hogan Hansen, according to The Detroit News. “Be smart, use your head, and just play your tail off.”

Those who have played in this rivalry know how ugly it can get. Whether it’s Devin Bush digging his heels into the Spartan logo in East Lansing, the brawl in the tunnel just a few years ago, or the countless other moments in this decades-long heated rivalry, fans can expect a nasty, hate-filled battle whenever these two teams face off.

But Kyle Whittingham made the point in his press conference this week that 55 players on the roster had never played in this rivalry, and the coaching staff itself has extremely limited experience in the animosity that exists between these two programs. The head coach told the media that he was bringing in some former players, like Jansen, to speak to the importance of this game and the vitriol that comes along with it.

Evan Link told The Detroit News, “(Jansen) kind of just reminded us where the onus lies in this game. It’s on the O line, it’s on the D line. Whoever controls that battle, whoever wins the rushing battle, wins the game.” That’s factual, because 49 of the last 56 in this contest have been won by the team with more rushing yards. It’s an area where the Wolverines have struggled to dominate on the offensive side all season.

That physicality often crosses a line, and the Wolverines are expecting that again this year. Jyaire Hill may have had the comment of the week. “Oh, yeah. I’m ready for (chippy plays),” cornerback Jyaire Hill shared with Angelique Chenglis. “Yeah, ready to twist some helmets. Yeah, I’m ready.”

National Perspective: Josh Pate puts Michigan on upset watch vs MSU

Pate commented on how Michigan got a great performance from true freshman Tommy Carr but still struggled to put Rutgers away. “I’m not counting on Michigan to get margin on anyone this year. Even the games they win, they are close games. That means I have to put at least a 6 (out of 10) on the upset alert concern meter for all Michigan games… Michigan State has no business beating Michigan, but yet, they’ve done it when they have no business doing it in the past.”

Portnoy: I’m petrified about Saturday’s game

I think this one speaks to how most Michigan faithful feel deep down about this one:

“Are we in the trust tree here? I am petrified about Saturday’s game” –@stoolpresidente talking about Michigan State vs Michigan pic.twitter.com/0nR8UrOZ9t

michigan.headline: Preview: Michigan State 2026
michigan.body:
Preview: Michigan State 2026

Seth
November 7th, 2026 at 6:00 AM

Essentials
WHAT
Michigan (5-3, 2-3) vs MSU (2-6, 0-5)

WHERE
Michigan Stadium, Ann Arbor, MI
WHEN
7:30 PM Saturday
THE LINE
M –14 (Vegas)
M –15 (SP+)
TELEVISION
Peacock/NBCSN
PBP: Paul Burmeister
Color: Yogi Roth (yay!)
TICKETS
From $112 (wear blue).
WEATHER
Chilly: High 40s for tailgating,
35° at halftime, winds 7-12 mph.
Overview
Pat Fitzgerald won a settlement against his former school, rendering it the judgment of the law that all parties agree Northwestern spun up the hazing scandal just to fire him. Most Big Ten athletics departments would look at a program going to such lengths to be rid of an alumnus who punched well above his weight at a serious academic for sixteen years and wonder what's really wrong with him. Michigan State, which just ran off evidently competent normal human Jonathan Smith in two years, only wanted to know how much Pat blamed Michigan.
The answer, since he got the job, is definitely "For all of it." Find the right message board and you will discover former Northwestern OL coach Kurt Anderson, a Michigan alum, and coaches loyal to retired DC Mike Hankwitz, a Michigan alum, were the only staff to keep their jobs after the hazing non-gate. Also Connor Stalions, burgers, and the fact that everything wrong with college football today has to do with money and lawyers, and we all know where those come from.
"Everything wrong with football" right now includes Michigan having to start a freshman AGAIN after misplaying a five-star quarterback investment. It's also starting to look like it means being saddled with a coach that Utah was trying to put out to pasture, and his nincompoop coordinator, because waiting for the last season to end before hiring a new staff means missing the window to have a roster for him. That's on top of administrators that can burn through $80 million in whoopsies, receive a $7 million parachute, and do absolutely nothing for four months while the TV guys stick a November Michigan-Michigan State game at 7:30 PM on a streaming network nobody subscribes to. A lot of that really is our fault. Pat's a good fit for MSU in the same way Kyle's a good fit for Michigan: neither of these are compliments.
Playing this game after basketball has started really takes the juice out of a rivalry that's less about bragging rights than making the other guy shut up. Fortunately the late date also provides more clarity for which of us is about to go quiet. Michigan's at that point in a 7- or 8-win season when the thing that's broken is unsalvageable and the thing that's working is still trying to win football games. State's in another kind of bad where one's roster has already been ravaged by injuries, bounced NIL checks, and four regime changes since COVID, and not everyone who went home for the bye week has come back.
[AFTER THE JUMP: They'd better bring a lot of hate.]

Run Offense vs MSU

Please be poses. [Bryan Fuller]
State's run defense was in the "eh, okay" range early in the season, but things have been trending down with each brutal injury. Middle linebacker Jordan Hall had an average depth of tackle of 1.3 yards, and an average depth of target of 1.2 yards when accumulated arm and lower body injuries took him out of the lineup in Game 4. Every other inside linebacker for MSU is a transfer who's least two yards worse in both categories, and  has a major hole in his game besides. Cam Stodghill from Albany tends to find the wrong gap. Buffalo transfer Dion Crawford can find his gap but not his zone. Auburn/Maryland vagabond Caleb Wheatland is more of miscast SAM than a true LB. Actual SAM Brady Pretzlaff was a decent recruit, but doesn't know what the playcall is half the time.
The defensive line was holding up them up as far the first snap at UCLA, when nose tackle Ben Roberts was carted off. By far MSU's best lineman, the dropoff has been severe. Fellow DT Eli Coenen was already a problem, and the backups are third- and second-year projects not ready for the workload. Ventures beyond them in the depth chart have looked like Michigan's attempts to use Cam Brandt. Their last saving grace has been safeties Nikai Martinez and Devin Vaught have been good at keeping those chunk gains from becoming full-blown explosives.
Against any other Michigan run game in my lifetime I'd say this sets up like a slow-motion paving. Unfortunately Jason Beck managed to blow the easiest "add a QB run game to a top-25 run offense that returns almost everybody" assignment in offseason history, and Michigan now doesn't have a base. They tried to do a lot of inside zone against Rutgers, but an injured OL wasn't getting consistent push, and once Rutgers pinched it the backs/receivers couldn't punish that with bounces. They don't run gap at all; the coaches apparently don't know how to teach more than the basics of stretch; and the jet/QB stuff had to be dropped.
Even a banged up MSU can get stuffs when you're spending half of your snaps with a Rhino on the field who doesn't know when the snap is coming. Expect this to be another slog, hopefully broken up by the occasional trucking by a running back playing at home in a rivalry game.
KEY MATCHUP: EVEN JASON BECK COULDN'T vs EVEN JASON BECK COULD. Wink Martindale had some doozies—including one in this rivalry—but even he knew how to club a baby seal. I don't know how bad Beck can go since Jordan Marshall and Savion Hiter rushing for 3.04 YPC against Rutgers must be some kind of world record. Blitzball tactics excepted, if Beck can't manage 5.0 YPC for his RBs against the broken bits of Spartan remains I'm giving credence to the conspiracists.
Pass Offense vs MSU

This too is passing. [Fuller]
It's hard to draw too many conclusions from Tommy Carr's first 2.5 starts except "kid has poise" and "kid was definitely committed to Miami (no not THAT Miami) one year ago." Much of his 10+ YPA against Rutgers came from events like throwing late to Salesi Moa and watching Rutgers decline to tackle him, or scrutinizing an open Mason Bonner in the middle of the field for a solid two seconds. Things that Tommy has shown that aren't wholly Rutger-dependent include perfectly placed "Go Get It!" balls to JJ Buchanan and scrambling opportunities earned from stepping up past the rush. Perfectly mediocre passing attacks have been made of less.
In contrast to their run defense, which was downright adequate before they lost the best two players in their front seven, State's pass defense started at Rutger-bad and then added Spartan injury misfortune. They had hopes a bye week would get some guys healthy again, but the latest availability report lists both Charles Brantley and fellow starter Tre Ball OUT. Brantley moved some jerseys when he transferred back from Miami (yes THAT Miami), got himself benched earlier this year, then returned okay. The nonconference revelation who usurped his spot—Tyran Chappell—hasn't played since Notre Dame in Week 3, and remains on the "Questionable" list. This means State is probably running out NiJhay Burt, a depth up-transfer they didn't have to play last year, and freshman Jeremiah Favorite for Brantley's spot. In NEVER FORGET terms, this is like being down to James Rogers and a true freshman Courtney Avery, except they're both 5-foot-11.
Alex found no issue with nickel Michael Richard and previously liked oft-injured field safety Nikai Martinez, while Vaught (if healthy) has a solid PFF score. Vaught wasn't targeted much in the games I went through—his interception was a gift—so I don't have much to add about his coverage except I don't know why PFF adores it while showing a lot of yards generated over the deep middle. Fellow 2023 transfer Aveon Grose is somehow still around as well.
If there's a meaningful difference from Tommy's last opponent, Alex thought MSU has at least one bona fide pass-rusher in RUSH edge Kenny Soares.
On the season, Soares has a team-leading 24 pressures, ten more than any other player on the team, and his two sacks ranks second on the squad. Here was a near-sack from the Notre Dame game, that Tommy Carr's big bro somehow escaped from:
Not great tackling, I know, but I liked showing a play in which Soares was able to beat a tackle on a national title contending team. Soares has dropped into coverage 41 times on the year, per PFF's charting, and has an interception, which was a sweet, acrobatic play.

Soares was a 2022 DE/OLB prospect from Connecticut that Don Brown was looking at for Michigan once upon a time. He wound up at Northwestern with an Anto Saka (another Brown fave) comp, and a first-call type of pickup when Fitzgerald's MSU number was activated, so there's some more juice there than the typical Spartan from the 800s. He's also small, had his development interrupted by a transfer to NC State, and is still more "EDGE" than lineman, so as long as Evan Link can get his hands on the little guy it shouldn't be that much of an issue.
KEY MATCHUP: JJ BUCHANAN vs IF WE SIT ON THEIR FACES AND ALL SORTS OF PLACES. This doesn't have to be complicated. One of those "5-11" cornerbacks is going to have Andrew Marsh. The other is going to have JJ Buchanan. Throw ball at large man.
Run Defense vs MSU

Do any of you guys want to try carrying it around? [Barron]
Try to find someone who loves you like Alex Drain loves the little ball of hate running backs that MSU finds every offseason.
4. Michigan State
One can argue the most exciting piece of Pat Fitzgerald's first team in East Lansing may be transfer RB Cam Edwards of UConn. This is the second time in recent memory that the Spartans have fished an intriguing UConn back out of the portal, but I think Edwards has more upside than Nate Carter did. Edwards was the bellcow for the Huskies last season, rushing for 1,240 yards, good for 15th in the FBS last season, and he did it with 15 TDs as well. He also added 187 receiving yards as the all-around offensive engine for UConn and I would expect him to be the engine for State this fall.
Fitzgerald even grabbed a respectable #2 back out of the portal in snagging Jaziun Patterson of Iowa, who rushed for 296 yards on 4.9 YPC behind Moulton last season. Patterson should be capable of reprising such a role behind Edwards and the duo of those two players is enough to rank the Spartans pretty highly on this list, bolstered by Patterson's star power.

Bad news, Alex: your UConn Joique Bell du jour isn't available for this game. Neither is FFFF Dangerman Patterson, nor even emergent 3rd string back Marvis Parrish, who got the start in their absence against UCLA. MSU is now down to former Nebraska walk-on Kenneth Williams, who has 19 carries for 71 yards, no TDs, and a fumble this year. He is slight—more slot shaped than RB—and if he went by Ken his entire name would be on his nameplate.

Most of those carries were late when UCLA had a three-score lead and MSU was just trying to get to the bye week. In competitive play the only thing I could learn watching Williams is he was ROUGH in pass-pro. Next is last year's third back Brandon Tullis, who was MSU's RB3 last year, and is more or less total walk-on territory if Williams wasn't already.
They may as well use their slots as RBs, since OC Nick Sheridan learned zone from Rich Rodriguez and has been plugging it in wherever he's gone since. That was along for the ride with Kalen DeBoer, mostly, until Alabama fans needed someone to blame for DeBoer not being Nick Saban. One thing Sheridan does have going for him that most MSU coordinators haven't is an offensive line that doesn't suck. My favorite offseason hot take was a majority of MSU's OL was better than their Oregon counterparts, and it's been a fun victory lap until now. LT Ben Murawski (a longtime starter at UConn) and NDSU center Trent Fraley were both dudes to Drain. LG Connor Moore was a solid up-transfer last year, and T Rakeem Johnson has been okay as a light swingman though he'd be better used outside. If there was a cyan here I might have given it to South Carolina transfer Nick Sharpe, who's 6'2"/351 but plays like he's 251 sometimes. They're best at running off Murawski.
"Best" is relative. MSU's rush offense this year has managed to climb to respectable against middling defenses but was shut down by anyone with a pulse—2.8 YPC vs Wisconsin, 3.4 vs Notre Dame—even when healthy. Squinting at numbers it looks like most of the variation comes to whether end-arounds gained or lost seven yards that week.
Michigan's defense front isn't watertight, but it was one of the better in the country at preventing more than a trickle of yards until Rutgers sprung some holes that my UFR attributed to young DE play. Word is the starting edges are back and Etta was left off the injury report entirely, which moves the young DEs back to backup work and the too young DEs back to the bench.
KEY MATCHUP: ALEX'S INFINITE LOVE FOR RUNNING BACKS vs TACKLING. Every week it feels Alex is giving mad respect to a running back, which given Alex's history probably just means Michigan's been facing a lot of good running backs. If that's the case, this is the week for Michigan's tackling numbers to swing back to decent.
Pass Defense vs MSU

Let's get this done quickly. [Barron]
This should be a potato mashing, after MSU got a bye and Michigan came back the healthier. Word is all three of John Henry Daley, Dominic Nichols, and Rod Moore are back. Meanwhile a murderer's row of if-Jeremiah-wasn't-around receivers have come and gone through Michigan's secondary with little more to show than a smattering of bad officiating and a big day from Penn State's Chase Sowell. Since then KJ Duff, Charlie Becker and Nick Marsh have combined for 5 catches for 57 yards. We'll always have that touchdown against Bama, but I think if that Fredrick Moore breakout is ever going to happen, it's probably not this week.
MSU's other receiving weapons are more in the Tony Diaz/Isaiah Sategna mold, IE slot-sized buggers who try to make hay in space. Slot receiver Chrishon McCray has been leading MSU in receiving but with an average depth of target of 7.6 yards. PFF reports no drops from him this year, and the 5th year Kent State transfer knows how to work his way open in a zone, but as long as Smith Snowden remains on his feet I think he can handle McCray. Joining Moore outside, Rodney Bullard is a 6th year Valdosta State transfer with a long eligibility and injury story to tell, but not much production to show for it. A converted slot, Bullard's been fine at catching things thrown at him, but doesn't often bail his quarterbacks out (1/4 on contesteds this year).
Those QBs could use some bailing. MSU gave up on the Aidan Chiles rollercoaster midseason last year and settled in for 2.5 years of Alessio Milivojevic. If healthy—a big "if" since he left the UCLA game and is questionable this week—Milivojevic is fine underneath but tends to leave downfield meat on the bone. Alex:
So let's talk about Milivojevic. On the season, the stats look okay, if pedestrian. Milivojevic has 1,263 yards to his name, completing 65.4% of passes for 6.8 Y/A. The strictures and conventions of sportswriting compel me to predict: Michigan is a middling team made up of a very good defense and an offense hopelessly broken by coaching malpractice. This makes them vulnerable to any other middling Big Ten team, but probably not this Michigan State, which was tracking medium-bad before the injuries and needed some of those to disappear during the bye to avoid really bad.
The demons are not hard to summon. Rutgers showed it is possible for even Jay Hill's defense to crack more than once in 60 minutes. Any hope of the run game finding a new base flittered away with a failure to iterate Stretch against IU. The dream of anything better than freshman-caliber quarterbacking this year died in the opener. Relative to reasonable expectations after 2025, and not counting pandemics, 2026 is easily the most disappointing Michigan football season of my life. I can imagine any number of ways the offense fails. I could also see their Iowa punter offsetting solid margins in yardage and 1st downs.
What I can't summon—at least with normal reason where events follow the things that precede them—is how MSU can move the ball with any consistency today. They can't pound away like Minnesota nor dink away like IU, nor chuck it at a contested baller like PSU or Rutgers. State's offense is at its best when Milivojevic can standing clean in the pocket and pick a little receiver who won a matchup. That's a good recipe for carving up explosives-prone Northwestern, but it takes an Ohio State-caliber suite of skill position players to play that way against a man defense of Michigan's caliber.

Pat Fitzgerald has a Jason Eck-caliber trick play that is MSU's largest gain by some margin.
It's annoyingly close until JJ Buchanan's second touchdown is the universal signal we can all go home/to bed.
Michigan, 19-8.

michigan.body:
MGoTarot Reading: Michigan State 2026
MGoTarot
November 7th, 2026 at 2:35 AM

MGoTarot is a fun predictive tool that I started after the Covid season to see if the cards were more interesting than the football. Thus began one of the great runs of Michigan football. The tarot card readings turned out to be pretty accurate and insightful in revealing the outcomes and energies of each game. There is no religion involved. Sometimes the cards rely on sacred imagery to inspire a deeper meaning. Tarot is closer to a pseudo-science with a weekly hypothesis, experiment, and theory. Over time, maybe we can tap into the emotional tapestry that the fandom, or MGoCollective brings every Saturday or maybe it’s just a big old exercise in pareidolia. Either way, it’s supposed to be simple fun. Feel free to comment with additional insights you might notice or offer a breakdown of the Hebrew letters found on the cards.

The approach is a standard 3 card spread showing elements of the past, the present, and the future outcome. Each card tells a story and together they form a larger story based on their positions. I do the reading within 24 hours of the game for accuracy. The method is to shuffle the cards while singing the Victors. I then lay out all the cards face down in a line and select 3 with my eyes closed using my off hand. This process helps to double randomize the deck so I am not selecting the same cards repeatedly like a poorly shuffled deck of Uno. I like to use the Salvador Dali Deck because it puts a modernist/art-history twist on the traditional 78 card Rider-Waite Deck. Plus the cards continue to have an oil-paint smell that is totally groovy.

"I remember when you were born. It was horrific"

From Ace to Two, and back to Ace, these coin cards keep popping up. After holding off Rutgers with primal talent, Michigan ran out the clock for another win. We last saw the Ace of Coins for the Penn State game. Both games featured top defense with just enough Tommy Carr to get the job done. Because of the anatomy symbolism in the card, this is a great representation of a talented true freshman being birthed into the world and refining his game. With the Death Card in last week’s spread, I thought we might see some changes to the offense or coaching staff. Like the confusion that swirled in the cards last year, we might not know the exact details until after Ohio State. So for now, put a mental asterisk next to that Death Card.

Sparti is as Sparti does. All hail the king, baby

Going into the Michigan State game, we are greeted by Salvador Dali himself as the King of Coins. The King is surrounded by luxury and even a pet ocelot (just like on Archer). Despite the wealth and talents, the King is also connected to his artistic roots via the fingerprints and by the cave drawing above his head. This is the perfect card for Michigan in this game. It is a reminder that Michigan is its own greatest resource. But there is also a warning associated with this card to not take wealth and talent for granted. Sparti is always on the hunt for an upset in this game. Michigan has won four in a row and is probably due for an upset. Given this card, Michigan is quite aware of the situation and should be ready to handle all the tricks and shenanigans Pat Fitzgerald can muster with a depleted roster.

"Sir, this is a highway median. It cannot be your 'Walden."

For the last 2 weeks we have had red cards for red teams. This week, we have a green card for a green team. The traditional meaning of the Nine of Wands is a pause before re-entering battle. Dali has thin-sliced the moment and turned it into a Waldenesque meditation of self-discovery. A lone huntsman stalks through the forest under the cathedral canopy of nature. Also featured on the card is the Green Man. He is a traditional artistic symbol of spring rebirth and growth. Being autumn, he’s not looking so hot. Dali depicts him as being sickly and depleted as he reaches out towards the huntsman. Could that be poor Michigan State and their injury depleted roster making sad gestures in the direction of Michigan? Could it be Michigan’s sadly anemic offense that cannot seem to get out of its own way and has endangered the Whittingham era in its first season? At this point, we have a good idea of what makes up Team 147. What is interesting is that this week’s cards seem to be headed in a different direction. We do not have the frustration of the Ten of Swords that doomed Underwood. We also do not have a replay of last week’s Death Card. The Nine of Wands is a reminder that we only have so many football games in a year. Instead of lamenting the state of Whittingham and Jason Beck’s offense, remember that the journey is the destination and for one night just enjoy beating the brakes off of Sparti…well, assuming you can find the game hidden away on Peacock.

November 6th, 2026 at 8:55 PM

This game may be our wake up call that it really is Fall! We've had such warm weather for so many Saturdays - we're going to be a lot closer to normal this week. A low pressure system exiting eastward out of the Great Lakes region kept plenty of clouds, scattered showers, and a breeze around Friday. Isolated showers may linger into Saturday morning and cloud cover will continue to be in place for the first part of the day before we see some clearing as this system moves out. We'll also have a breezy NW wind, adding that extra chill to the air. Luckily by game time, we'll see partly cloudy skies, dry conditions, and a lighter wind. Grab the warm blue coat as temps will fall fast for this night game! Let's go guys, let's keep that trophy at home for the 5th time in a row!
Tailgating
Making a day out of it? Don't forget to pick your outfit wisely as it's the Blue Out! & fire up the crockpot oatmeal - this is one of those stick-to-your-ribs type of breakfast days! You'll want the xl size coffee as well, and no judgement if you reach the tailgate site and add a little something extra to it. Morning temperatures will be in the lower 30s, but a brisk NW wind will have it feeling like the mid 20s! We'll start the day with some cloud cover and the slim chance of a few showers. Choosing to sleep in and show up at lunchtime? By then temps will be in the mid to upper 40s. NW winds will remain steady around 15mph with gusts into the low 20s (enough of a breeze to sway small trees) - making it feel more like the low 40s or so. Cloud cover will decrease during the afternoon as we hit highs around 50. Winds will also start to lighten, shifting to the W, and into the evening hours we'll lose the gusts completely. The Wolverine Walk is around 5:15pm, which should look beautiful with some lingering clouds. This is the Military Appreciation game, so if you'd like, you can share photos of loved ones in our armed forces using #MGoTroops. You might want to do that while you have better cell service. Reminder the sunset time is now around 5:20pm, so make sure you have a way to light up your site as you're packing up! Is this when you wear the hat with the little light on it, showing everyone how great it is that you can see and use two hands? :D If you want to make sure you can still see and feel your hands by the end of the game, you might want to put a couple of those little warmers in your pockets before heading for the gates.
Kickoff
43 degrees for the kickoff with some clouds across the sky! Westerly winds will be around 10mph - enough to move the smaller twigs on the trees - putting wind chills closer to 40. This isn't a bad game to get in there early! There is recognition of Michigan football alumni, so over 150 alumni will be lined up to bring the players onto the field. Also, large flags representing the six military branches will be displayed on the field during the national anthem.
Halftime
Taking a hot chocolate break? By the half, temps will be in the upper 30s! Our W wind will be around 7-8mph, just enough to keep the leaves rustling about and make it feel more like the mid 30s. The Marching Band's show features songs from the 2010s - think Maroon 5 and One Direction. Did you notice the flags around the stadium? American flags will be flown around the stadium in honor of individuals who have served or are serving in our armed forces.
Post-Game
Seeing some stars on and off the field as we walk out of the Big House with the win! Nice to have you staying at home, Paul. It's a chilly end to the game with temps in the mid 30s and wind chills in the lower 30s. Winds will stay around 5-7mph overnight, gradually shifting to the SW. We'll drop a few more degrees by the time the lights come on, and although we don't have much of a wind, that breeze will be enough to have it feeling more like the upper 20s. Maybe wait inside for that Uber home - brrr! The plus side to having a SW to W wind is that it helps to bring in some warmer air for Sunday. Afternoon highs will be in the upper 50s with some sunshine the second half of the weekend. Let's go blue!!

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The um wolverines
msu.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches practice at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor ahead of the game between Michigan and Oklahoma on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation.  This column has been away for a few weeks with a bye last week and the game against UCLA before that, which does not have an SB Nation site.  But we are back for our in-state hate game.  I sat down with Von Lozon of Maize N Brew for a quick look at this weekend’s opponent.  Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: UM is in the first year under head coach Kyle Whittingham. Did that hire take you by surprise? Aside from any surprise, what were your thoughts on the hire? What were your expectations for this season in terms of performance and record?

Von Lozon:  I wasn’t surprised, but I was skeptical of the hire simply due to his age and me wondering how much he had left in the tank. I never thought he was a bad coach or anything like that — if anything, I thought he was one of the more underrated coaches in the country — but I was a little nervous about how things would translate at Michigan and in the Big Ten. I thought this team’s ceiling heading into the year was 9-3, which they can still technically reach, but I would be incredibly shocked if that happened.

TOC: Your season opener came down to a famously controversial ending. I won’t ask you for your thoughts on how that played out. But I would like to know how much panic you had after that first game? After that 1st game, UM was expected to lose their 2nd game against Oklahoma. How did that win reshape your expectations?

VL: Given my offseason skepticism, I was really worried following the WMU game. But then the Wolverines beat Oklahoma the very next week and I was thinking to myself, “Okay, maybe that is more of what we should expect.” And then the next week, Michigan was in a first-half dog fight against UTEP, so at that point, I knew this would be a team that plays up (and down) to its competition. That has continued every week all season, as the only game that wasn’t a one-score affair was that UTEP game. Needless to say, it’s been a roller coaster of a year for Michigan.

TOC: Whittingham has made a switch at QB, with Tommy Carr taking over a couple games ago as the starter. What do you think went wrong with Bryce Underwood? Should the switch have been made sooner? What do you like about Carr’s game that makes him better than Underwood?

VL: It’s a really curious case, right? Underwood flashed his potential at times during his freshman season, but he looked even more lost this year before the coaching staff made the change. It’s interesting, especially considering all the reports coming out of fall camp were that Underwood had improved under the new coaching staff’s direction and should take a sophomore leap. But his freshman tendencies (staring down one receiver, bailing out of the pocket too soon, etc.) came back to haunt him this season, resulting in far too many negative plays and turnovers.

I do think the switch should have been made during the game at Minnesota, but admittedly, that would have been a really tough spot to put a freshman quarterback in the game for the first time. The thing I like so far about Carr is his poise. He hasn’t let anything phase him too much yet — even though he struggled at the start of the Indiana game with a couple of turnovers, he kept his head down, kept working and eventually put Michigan in a good position to win (thanks a lot, Jason Beck!).

TOC: Tell us about the Wolverine defense. What is the base formation? What level of the D is the best? What player do the MSU coaches most need to game plan for?

VL: The defense is by far the best part of this football team. Jay Hill runs a true 4-3 defensive scheme with the linebackers playing off the ball. The wrinkle is that one of the linebackers can be a bit of a hybrid player at times. Depending on the call, that linebacker can be up on the line of scrimmage setting the edge or dropping into the box. It gives Michigan’s defense some flexibility without needing to change personnel. Look for Chase Taylor (No. 4), who has been in this role quite a bit this year, as well as MIKE linebacker Troy Bowles (No. 18).
The best level of the defense is the defensive line. Michigan can rotate edge rushers like John Henry Daley, Dom Nichols, Nate Marshall, Benny Patterson III, and true freshmen Tariq Boney and Carter Meadows without a real drop-off. The interior group of Trey Pierce, Enow Etta and Jonah Lea’ea has been solid as well. That depth lets them stay fresh and keep the pressure on for four quarters.

The player MSU needs to game plan for is Daley. He missed last week’s game due to an injury, but he is expected to play this weekend. He leads the team in sacks (4) and also has 6.5 tackles for loss. When he has been on the field, he has been Michigan’s best edge rusher. Nichols is right behind him, and the two of them together are why the defense can get to the quarterback so often without blitzing.

TOC: Fill in the blank: UM will win if ___________.  UM will lose if ___________.

VL: U-M will win if they avoid turning the ball over, run the ball well (AKA: go on long drives that drain the clock), and score touchdowns, not field goals, in the red zone.

U-M will lose if they turn the ball over, give up some explosive plays to MSU’s offense (much like vs Rutgers last week), and take MSU lightly. On that last point, I’m a little worried these guys don’t really know a whole lot about this rivalry. Kyle Whittingham has said multiple times that this game is important, but it isn’t the most important rivalry game Michigan has. Savion Hiter said all he knows about this game is that the rivalry is “dirty.” I really have not enjoyed hearing the things that some of these guys have said throughout the week, so I really, really hope Michigan doesn’t take MSU for granted.

TOC: Predict the final score.

VL: Michigan 20, Michigan State 17.
